hints: Focus on the two clues in order, first the metal reacting with water to make a hydroxide solution, then that solution reacting with sulfuric acid to make a sulfate.
Remember that metal plus water gives a metal hydroxide, so adding sulfuric acid will then try to make the metal sulfate, ask yourself which sulfate is insoluble.
Recall the classic white precipitate test for sulfate ions and think which of these four metals forms a sulfate that does not dissolve.
walkthrough:
**What does reaction with water make?**

Metals that react with water form a metal hydroxide solution plus hydrogen gas. All four metals here would give a colourless hydroxide solution.

General equation:
$$\text{M} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{metal hydroxide} + \text{H}_2$$

**What happens when we add sulfuric acid?**

The hydroxide solution reacts with $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to form the metal sulfate plus water. Whether we see a precipitate depends only on whether that sulfate is soluble.

General equation:
$$\text{metal hydroxide} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{metal sulfate} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Use sulfate solubility rules**

This is the key test. Most Group 1 sulfates like $\text{K}_2\text{SO}_4$ and $\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4$, and $\text{MgSO}_4$, are very soluble so they stay colourless in solution. Barium sulfate, $\text{BaSO}_4$, is famously insoluble and forms a thick white precipitate.

**Identify metal T**

Only barium gives both observations, a soluble hydroxide $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ then an insoluble sulfate $\text{BaSO}_4$.

Specific equations for barium:
$$\text{Ba} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Ba(OH)}_2 + \text{H}_2$$
$$\text{Ba(OH)}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(s) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

options.A: Barium reacts with water to give soluble, colourless barium hydroxide, Ba(OH)2. With sulfuric acid this gives insoluble white barium sulfate, BaSO4, which is the observed white precipitate. This matches both statements perfectly.
options.B: Magnesium reacts only very slowly with cold water, and its hydroxide Mg(OH)2 is sparingly soluble. More importantly, magnesium sulfate, MgSO4, is soluble, so no white precipitate would form with sulfuric acid.
options.C: Potassium reacts vigorously with water to give colourless soluble KOH, but potassium sulfate, K2SO4, is soluble. No precipitate forms, so the second observation fails. Students sometimes pick this because Group 1 metals react fast with water.
options.D: Sodium reacts vigorously with water to give colourless soluble NaOH, but sodium sulfate, Na2SO4, is soluble. No precipitate forms, so the second observation fails. Like potassium, it is a trap for focusing only on the first reaction.
